1.pericope_label: Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal — continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving

schools.summary: Object first to the chapter division, since this verse properly belongs to the preceding chapter and it is strange that those who divided the chapters and verses should have separated it from what it manifestly belongs to and begun a new chapter with it, when it has no connection with what follows. Then explain the second term as distributive rather than arithmetical right, regulated and proportioned according to the circumstances, station or calling of individuals; and bring masters under control, since looking down as it were from aloft they despise the condition of servants and think themselves bound by no law, whereas both parties are equally under subjection to the authority of God. On the prayer, admit that no exact order is to be expected in these general exhortations, since otherwise he would have begun with prayer; and find two things commended, assiduity and alacrity, the first exhorting to perseverance and the second set against coldness and listlessness and against proceeding in the duty as a mere form. Deny that continuance means being always formally at prayer, or that saints are always in praying frames of soul, however desirable such frames may be: it intends frequency and constancy, in opposition both to an entire omission of the duty and to a performance of it now and then, since Christians are not bound to stated hours as the Jews were and yet a day should not pass without it. And explain the thanksgiving as a guard, since God must be solicited for present necessity in such a way that we do not meanwhile forget favours already received, and we ought not to be so importunate as to murmur and take offence if he does not immediately gratify our wishes, but must receive contentedly whatever he gives.

Join the verse to the foregoing chapter as part of that discourse, and then require justice of masters — not only strict justice but equity and kindness: be faithful to your promises and perform your agreements, defrauding servants of nothing and not keeping back by fraud the hire of the labourers; require no more of them than they are able to perform, and lay no unreasonable burdens on them beyond their strength; provide what is fit, supply proper food and physic, and allow such liberties as may fit them the better for cheerful service and make it easier to them — and this though they be employed in the meanest and lowest offices, and be of another country and of a different religion from yourselves. Give the reason as a rule of measure: you who are masters of others have a Master yourself and are the servants of another Lord, not lords of yourselves but accountable to one above you, so deal with your servants as you expect God should deal with you. Then connect the next verse backwards, making it part of the duty masters owe their servants to pray with them, and to pray daily with them, being concerned for their souls as well as their bodies, since they are parts of your charge and under your influence. And press the duty on everyone: keep up your constant times of prayer without being diverted by other business, keep the heart close to the duty without wandering or deadness and even to the end of it, lay hold of all opportunities and choose the fittest seasons, those least liable to disturbance from other things; and let thanksgiving have a part in every prayer.

Print the outline of the household code so that its third division plainly ends at this verse. Note that the apostle changes from a neuter adjective with the article for the abstract idea to an abstract substantive found only here and in one other epistle, and remark that if employers always did this there would be no labour problem. Take the persons meant to be bondmen, whose time and services were at their masters’ disposal and who could not enforce their just and equal claims by an appeal to the laws, and who were therefore dependent on the equity and kindness of their masters; hold that not a few converted to the faith were held in involuntary servitude, that the apostles did not design a violent disruption of these bonds or mean to lead slaves to rise against their masters, but that they meant to represent the condition as hard and undesirable, to instruct slaves to embrace the earliest opportunity of freedom that offered, and to lay down such principles as would lead masters to emancipate their slaves and so ultimately to abolish the thing itself. Read the closing clause as a wholesome reminder that the Master in heaven keeps his eye on the conduct of masters here towards those they employ. Then take the prayer: do not neglect it, observe it at all stated times, maintain the spirit of it and embrace all proper occasions; and divide the watching three ways, watching for favourable opportunities, watching that the mind may be in a right frame when you pray, and watching that when the mind is in a right frame you may not neglect to pray. Add the philology, that the verb for continuing means to hold strongly to a thing and that the participle for watching is a late present formed on a perfect active stem.

Say that this verse should have been added to the preceding one and that the chapter should have begun with the exhortation to prayer; and give the argument of the whole chapter in order before beginning, from the duty of masters through the request for prayer, the walking wisely and the redeeming of time, the errand of the two messengers, the salutations from Rome, the letter to be exchanged with Laodicea, the direction to Archippus and the closing benediction. Distinguish the two terms as contract and surplus: just according to your contract, equitable even beyond the letter of your contract. Concede that the persons spoken of are bondmen or slaves, and find the exhortation the more evidently proper for it. Then make prayer the condition of every other duty in the chapter, since without it neither wives, husbands, children, parents, servants nor masters could fulfil what God requires of them in their several stations: all might and power and life come from God, his creatures are continually dependent on him, and to earnest persevering prayer he has promised every supply, but he who prays not has no promise. Ask how few wives feel it their duty to pray for grace to behave as wives, and how few husbands pray for the grace suited to their situation, and say the like of children and parents and servants and masters; for as every situation has its peculiar duties and trials, so to every situation there is a peculiar grace appointed, and the grace suited to a man as a member of society at large will not suffice him as a husband or a father or a master. Trace family unhappiness to the omission, since many proper marriages become unhappy because the parties never earnestly besought God for the grace necessary to them as husbands and wives — which is the origin of family broils in general.

debates: Whether this verse belongs to the previous chapter.
What the second term of the masters’ duty adds to the first.
What the apostles intended towards the institution of slavery.
What continuance in prayer requires.
What the watching is directed at.
outliers: Gill, Henry and Clarke all protest against the chapter division, and Ellicott’s outline silently agrees with them.
Calvin reads the word for equality as distributive right proportioned to station, not as sameness.
Barnes argues that the apostles meant to lay down principles that would abolish slavery without disrupting it violently.
Robertson turns the verse into a remark on modern industrial relations.
Clarke makes prayer the precondition of every domestic duty in the chapter and blames family quarrels on its neglect.
Calvin concedes that these exhortations follow no exact order.

3.pericope_label: Praying also for us, that God would open unto us a door of utterance — walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time

schools.summary: Take the request for prayer as genuine humility and not dissimulation under a guise of it, since the apostle was sensible of the greatness of the ministerial work and of his own imperfection and weakness, and of what advantage the prayers even of the meanest in the church might be to him; make it the duty of churches and of particular believers to pray for their ministers. Draw the consequence: who in the present day would dare to despise the intercessions of brethren, which the apostle openly declares himself to stand in need of, since it is not in vain that the Lord has appointed this exercise of love between us, so that each ought both to pray for his brethren and diligently to seek help from the prayers of others as occasion requires. Then refuse the inference some draw from it, that the dead are to be implored to pray for us, calling it worse than childish, since a man commending himself to the prayers of brethren with whom he has mutual fellowship by God’s commandment bears no resemblance to it. Say of the next clause that it sets the difficulty out more strongly, since what is asked is an undaunted confidence such as befits the majesty of the gospel, and make a rule of it, that we are not to give way to the fury of our adversaries but to strive even to death in the publication of the gospel — and, since this is beyond our power, to pray that the Lord may not leave us destitute of the spirit of confidence. Take the manifesting in a ministerial sense only, the thing being a mystery hidden in God from everlasting and wrapped during the legal dispensation in types and shadows and sacrifices, and still hidden from the natural man, since God alone by his Spirit makes it manifest in a spiritual and saving way. And give three reasons why regard is to be had to those outside rather than to believers: lest any stumbling-block be put before the blind, for nothing is readier to occur than that unbelievers are driven from bad to worse by our imprudence and their minds are wounded so that they hold religion more and more in abhorrence; lest occasion be given for detracting from the honour of the gospel, the name of Christ exposed to derision, persons rendered more hostile and persecutions stirred up; and lest, while we are mingled together in partaking of food and on other occasions, we be defiled by their pollutions and by little and little become profane — adding that intercourse with them is dangerous, and that amidst so great a corruption we must seize opportunities of doing good.

Explain the request simply, that the apostle earnestly desired liberty to preach the gospel and asked that it be restored to him, and identify what he calls the mystery with the mystery of the gospel named in the parallel epistle. Distinguish the figure carefully from its other occurrences: in those places the opened door is the door of external opportunity, whereas here the door of utterance is the removal of all internal impediments to preaching. Note the objective genitive, a door for preaching, and find it comforting to other preachers that the greatest of all preachers should ask prayer that he might be set free again to preach; observe that he is always conscious of this limitation, this chain, and that at bottom he is a prisoner because of his preaching to the Gentiles. Remark on the next clause that, wonderful as his preaching was to his hearers, he was never satisfied with it — and what preacher can be? Then make the wisdom towards outsiders a matter of reputation, since men of the world judge religion not from the profession but from the life of its friends, not from preaching or books or the conduct of its Founder but from what they see in the daily walk of the members of the church; they understand its nature well enough to know when its friends are inconsistent with their profession, and they set a higher value on honesty and integrity than on doctrines. Compare the parallel passage, where the same wisdom is set to guard against excess or recklessness within, whereas here it watches against external dangers and makes full use of external opportunities. And give the redeeming of the time its plainest sense: we all have the same time, and the apostle goes into the open market and buys it up by using it rightly, taking wise walking to win outsiders.

Urge that the success and spread of the gospel be ever dear to them, and that they pray fervently that it may have free course. Then trace the figure of the door through the other places where the same word stands for an entrance, occasion or opportunity to commence or perform a work — the door of faith opened to the Gentiles, the great and effectual door at Ephesus, the door opened at Troas — and note that the best Latin writers use the same metaphor, so that what is meant here is an occasion or opportunity for the doctrine of the gospel. Read the request also as utterance given, that the mouth may be opened boldly and an opportunity of speaking be granted such that none can hinder; and take the manifesting as a laying open, that all men may see it. Then, on walking wisely towards those who are without, explain the phrase from the figure of the Church as an enclosure, a field or vineyard hedged about, those outside not being under that especial protection which the followers of Christ have; derive the phrase about the pale of the Church from the stake that makes such an enclosure. Grant that the maxim of no salvation outside it is true wherever the doctrines of Christianity are preached, but deny the use made of it when one description of people professing Christianity, with their own peculiar mode of worship and creed, arrogates to itself exclusively the title of The Church and then reasons from a true maxim falsely understood.

Exhort to a prudent and decent conduct towards all with whom they converse, and especially towards those outside the Christian church among whom they live: be careful in all your dealings with them to get no hurt by them and to contract none of their customs, since evil communications corrupt good manners; and to do them no hurt either, neither increasing their prejudices against religion nor giving them occasion of dislike, but rather doing them all the good you can and by the fittest means and in the proper seasons recommending religion to them. Read the redeeming of the time either as improving every opportunity of doing them good and making the best use of your time in proper duty, since diligence in redeeming time much recommends religion to the good opinion of others, or else as walking cautiously and with circumspection, giving them no advantage against you nor exposing yourselves to their malice and ill-will, because the days are evil, that is, dangerous, and times of trouble and suffering.

Set the charge beside what Christ said to the disciples when he sent them as sheep among wolves and bade them be wise as serpents and harmless as doves: be upon your guard, giving them no handle against you. Mark the limitation, that against our own members we have no need of so much caution as against those without, since where brethren are there are many allowances and kindnesses, and it is not the same to be among enemies and foes as among friends. Then, having alarmed them, encourage them again, since the present time is short. And guard the counsel at once from being a counsel of craft, since to be crafty or hypocritical is no part of wisdom but of senselessness: in matters wherein they do you no harm, give them no handle, rendering to all their dues, tribute and custom and honour; let the Preaching alone be the ground of war and let that war have no other origin, for if we make enemies on other grounds we shall have no reward, they will become worse, and they will seem to have just complaints against us. Cite the apostle’s own submissiveness before a ruler where the Preaching was not at stake, since had he thought it his duty to insult him he would have spoiled everything; and cite the gentleness with which the first apostles answered that we must obey God rather than men, though men who had renounced their own lives might have insulted and done anything whatever — they had renounced their lives not to win vainglory but that they might preach and speak all things with boldness, the other course marking want of moderation.

debates: Whether the door asked for is outward opportunity or inward freedom of speech.
What follows from an apostle asking others to pray for him.
Why wisdom is enjoined towards outsiders in particular.
Whether the counsel of prudence risks becoming a counsel of craft.
What redeeming the time means here.
outliers: Ellicott separates this door from the doors of opportunity elsewhere and makes it the removal of internal impediments.
Calvin uses the verse against the invocation of departed saints, calling the inference worse than childish.
Clarke turns the phrase about those who are without into an excursus on the pale of the Church and its misuse.
Chrysostom guards the prudence explicitly against craft, and would have the preaching be the only ground of enmity.
Robertson finds it comforting that the greatest of preachers asked prayer for liberty to preach.
Calvin gives three distinct reasons for the caution, the third being fear of defilement by table fellowship.

6.pericope_label: Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt — all my state shall Tychicus declare unto you

schools.summary: Report that salt among the Greeks was the emblem of wit, and reject the gloss that would make the clause mean only courteous and agreeable rather than morose and melancholy — true so far as it goes and included in the rule, but not all that is meant, since the speech is to be imbued with the spirit of religion so as to show that the soul is under the influence of love to the Redeemer. Take the seasoning as wit outright, citing the classical author who uses salt of speech and the phrase about Attic salt, noting that not too much salt is meant and not too little, that our modern word for the indecent is this same word degenerated into vulgarity, and that grace and salt together make an ideal combination; and add, of the charge to know how to answer each man, the question who does know. Elsewhere hear the Lord’s own saying about salt behind the phrase, and the warning against corrupt words in the parallel epistle, but argue away from the preserving sense, since the context makes the use of the salt the teaching of how to answer every man, and that answer is to be given to those outside; so the seasoning is probably a provision against insipidity, agreeing to some extent with the classical usage, the speech being primarily with grace and kindled by the true life of Christian grace, and secondarily furnished with good sense and point so as to be effective for the inquirer or against the scoffer. On the messenger, compare the parallel epistle and note the same future verb and the same two descriptive epithets, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, with fellow-servant added here, which one commentator explains by the earlier use of that word of Epaphras, and suggest that the word faithful may govern both substantives and mean faithful to the apostle as well as to Christ. And prefer the reading that ye may come to know our affairs, an ingressive aorist subjunctive, against the third person singular, adding that the closing verb is properly rendered comfort here and not exhort.

Take the speech either as concerning grace, so that when saints meet they converse about the work of grace upon their souls, how it was begun and carried on and in what case it now is, and about the doctrines of grace, to instruct and build up one another — excluding thereby all obscene words, filthiness, foolish talking and jesting — or else as spoken in the exercise of grace, that is in truth and faithfulness and sincerity, without lying, dissimulation or flattery. Require suavity of speech, such as may allure the hearers by its profitableness, and condemn not merely communications openly wicked or impious but also such as are worthless and idle. Grant that profane men have their seasonings of discourse and that classical writers frequently use the term for witticisms, but refuse to speak of these; nay more, since witticisms are insinuating and for the most part procure favour, so that it is to be feared believers would addict themselves to them, indirectly prohibit their practice and familiar use, reckoning as tasteless everything that does not edify, and setting the word against talkativeness, taunts, and all sorts of trifles which are either injurious or vain — for the man who accustoms himself to caution in his communications will not fall into the absurdities into which prating persons fall. On the messenger, make the sending itself a pledge of the apostle’s concern: though he was in prison and in danger of his life, he made care for himself a secondary matter and consulted their interests, so that his singular zeal shines forth no less than his prudence, the body being under confinement while the mind, anxious to employ itself in everything good, roams far and wide. Find prudence also in the choice, since a fit and prudent person was sent to confirm them and withstand the craftiness of the false apostles, while Epaphras was retained beside him until they should learn what and how great an agreement there was in doctrine among all true teachers, hearing from the one what they had previously learned from the other. Add the biography of the messenger: an Asian by birth, whose name signifies fortunate and answers to a Latin name in another epistle, said to have been one of the seventy disciples and afterwards bishop of Chalcedon.

Take the salt in its preserving sense, as having a tendency to oppose and preserve from the corruption of sin, and quote the rabbinic saying that he who omits a word in prayer should begin again at the beginning, since he who does not is like boiled pottage in which there is no salt. Let all conversation be such as may exemplify and recommend Christianity, not only holy but wise and gracious and intelligent, since a harsh method of proposing or defending the doctrines of Christianity serves only to repel men from those doctrines and from the way of salvation. Note that salt, from its use in preserving food and rendering it savoury and wholesome, has always been made the emblem of wisdom, and that the term has been used of what is terse, comprehensive, useful, elegant and impressive in composition or conversation. Read the charge about answering as a direction that the discourse be so judiciously managed that they may discern how to treat the prejudices and meet the objections of both Jews and Gentiles. And on the messenger, say he well knew the apostle’s zeal and perseverance in preaching, his sufferings, his success in converting both Jews and Gentiles, and the converts made in Caesar’s household, so that he could give these in ample detail — some of which it would not have been prudent to commit to writing. Prefer also the reading that ye may know our affairs against that he may know yours, since he was sent not to learn their affairs but to carry the letter, make the apostle’s state known, and comfort their hearts by the news he brought, as the next verse confirms.

Observe that in closing the epistle the apostle does several of his friends the honour of leaving their names on record with some testimony of his respect, which will be spoken of wherever the gospel comes. Explain why he gives no account in writing of his present state: the bearer would deliver it by word of mouth more fully and particularly, and the churches cannot but be concerned for good ministers and desirous to know their state. Note the character given him, a beloved brother and faithful minister, and that a great apostle owns a faithful minister for a brother and a beloved brother, since faithfulness in anyone is truly lovely and renders him worthy of affection and esteem; note too the title of fellow-servant, since ministers are servants to Christ and fellow-servants to one another, having one Lord though different stations and capacities of service. And draw the standing lesson, that it adds much to the beauty and strength of the gospel ministry when ministers are loving and condescending one to another, and by all just means support and advance one another’s reputation.

Remark that the brevity of one short epistle alone availed to protect it against the falsifying hands of the heretic, and wonder that having received into his collection a letter written to a single man he should have rejected three others that all treat of ecclesiastical discipline — his aim being, one supposes, to carry the interpolating process even to the number of the apostle’s epistles. Then ask the reader to remember that proofs have here been adduced out of the apostle in support of subjects previously handled, and that the topics deferred to this portion of the work have now been brought to a close.

debates: Whether the salt is a preservative or a seasoning against dullness.
Whether wit in speech is commended or indirectly forbidden.
Whether the speech is to be about grace or in the exercise of grace.
Why the apostle sent a messenger instead of writing his news.
Whether the text reads that he may know your affairs or that you may know ours.
outliers: Calvin indirectly forbids the witticisms that Barnes, Clarke and Robertson all find commended in the same word.
Ellicott argues away from the preserving sense that Clarke builds his whole note on.
Robertson traces a modern word for indecency to the same root as the salt of the verse.
Clarke suggests that some of the news was too dangerous to commit to writing.
Calvin finds a doctrinal purpose in the apostle keeping one messenger back while sending another.
The block printed under Tertullian here is not about this epistle at all, but about Philemon and Marcion.

9.pericope_label: With Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you — Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister’s son to Barnabas

schools.summary: Doubt the usual identification of the second messenger, since it can scarcely be believed that this is the slave of Philemon, the name of a thief and a fugitive having been liable to reproach; and note that both men are distinguished by honourable titles so that the embassy may have the more weight and they may do the more good. Elsewhere supply what is known of him, that he had been a servant who ran away and was converted by the apostle, that he was afterwards bishop of Beroea, and that some say he suffered martyrdom under Domitian. Infer from the title of fellow-prisoner that others were made prisoners along with the apostle after he was brought to Rome, and judge it probable that his enemies at the outset exerted themselves to deter all pious persons from helping him by threatening them with the like danger, and that this had its effect for a time, until some gathered courage and despised everything held out to them in the way of terror. Note the manuscripts that differ over the mood of the verb about receiving, and explain the clause as expressing what the charge was that they had already received. Give the biography of the saluters where it helps: one a Macedonian and a Thessalonian, which does not hinder his being a Jew, since he might be born there of Jewish parents, and since the Jews themselves say that the names of most Israelites outside the land are as the names of strangers; another bearing a Hebrew name common among the Jews with a surname given to men remarkable for holiness. Say that few Jews at Rome showed themselves helpers of the gospel, nay that the whole nation was opposed to Christ, and that only those are meant who were endowed with the gifts necessary for promoting it. Then ask where the chief apostle was at that time, and answer that either he has been shamefully passed over here, and not without injustice, or else those speak falsely who maintain that he was then at Rome. And call the gospel the kingdom of God, since it is the sceptre by which God reigns over us and by it we are singled out to life eternal.

Identify the second messenger with the runaway of the other epistle, recently converted and warmly loved, and take the phrase about his being one of them to mean that he came from their own city and nation. Then argue from that phrase against the modern institution: would the apostle have addressed a community of masters and said of a runaway that he was one of them, and would a minister of the gospel in the Northern States, sending a letter by a runaway slave to masters in the South, say so, or would it be kindly received if he did? There is reason therefore to think his condition was not what the word now denotes. Call him co-bearer of the letter and praised on a par with his companion, runaway slave though he is, and take the words not as a reproach to the city for having such a man but as a privilege, that the church there might give a proper welcome to a returning converted slave and treat him as a brother. See in the two epithets a remarkable commentary on the rules for slaves and masters just laid down. On the saluters, trace the first through the tumult at Ephesus, the journey to Jerusalem and the voyage to Rome, where he is named as being with us; note that he is called a fellow-prisoner here while in the letter sent at the same time that title falls to another and he is merely a fellow-labourer, call the variation a characteristic mark of independence and genuineness in the epistles, and admit it can be accounted for only by conjecture, such as their alternately sharing the captivity — while reporting that one commentator argues for a literal imprisonment and that fellow-workers may have shared it voluntarily by turns. Settle the disputed word of kinship as cousin rather than nephew, which explains the earlier interest taken in the man; recall that he was once rejected for his defection in the work and is now cordially commended because he had made good again. Note that the Hebrew name of the last saluter is the common one and the surname its Latin equivalent, that the juxtaposition suggests the brethren who held aloof in strife and envy were themselves of the circumcision, and that the word for the comfort these three gave is a medical term from which our word for a soothing medicine descends.

Say that the second messenger was a native of Phrygia if not of the city itself, and being lately converted could give satisfactory information about the apostle’s state, which would be doubly acceptable as he was their countryman; note the manuscripts and versions that add a word to the clause about what is done here, and observe that these brethren could give an account of the transactions at Rome which it might not be prudent to commit to writing, the reign then current being not only cruel but suspicious, jealous and dangerous. On the fellow-prisoner, state the difficulty flatly: he is called a prisoner here and the other is not, while in the letter to Philemon the other is called a prisoner and he is not, so that one of them is wrong, though it is uncertain which, unless both were prisoners; suggest that as a zealous adherent who followed the apostle everywhere and ministered to him in prison he might have been imprisoned on that account, and that the two need not have been imprisoned at the same time, since providence might so order it that when one was in prison the other was at liberty. Note that although there had been some difference between the apostle and Mark, they were fully reconciled. Distinguish the last saluter’s Hebrew name from the name he bore among Greeks and Romans, and say that only these three, formerly Jews or proselytes, assisted in preaching, others preaching Christ from envy and strife in order to add affliction to the apostle’s bonds. Then draw the conclusion: it is evident that the chief apostle was not then at Rome, or he would certainly have been mentioned in this list, since we cannot suppose him in the list of those who preached from impure motives — and as it cannot be proved that he was ever bishop of that city, the keystone of the triumphal arch of the pope of Rome is pulled out, and the building of his supremacy cannot stand. Explain the tense of the directions by ancient usage, since the ancients adapted their language to the time of reading a letter and not, as we do, to the time of writing.

Draw the moral from the reconciliation: the apostle had differed with another over this Mark, yet he is not only reconciled but recommends him to the churches, which is an example of a truly Christian and forgiving spirit — if men have been guilty of a fault it must not always be remembered against them, and we must forget as well as forgive. Observe the comfort the apostle had in the communion of saints and ministers, one his fellow-servant, another his fellow-prisoner, and all his fellow-workers, working out their own salvation and endeavouring to promote the salvation of others; and that the effectual fervent prayer is the prevailing prayer and availeth much. And add the warning, that the smiles and flatteries and frowns of the world, the spirit of error, or the working of self-love, lead many to a way of preaching and living which comes far short of fulfilling their ministry, while those who preach the same doctrine and follow the same example may expect the divine favour and blessing.

debates: Whether the second messenger is the runaway slave of the other epistle.
What the phrase about his being one of them implies about his condition.
Which of the two companions was actually the apostle’s fellow-prisoner.
What the reconciliation with Mark teaches.
What follows from one apostle not being named among those at Rome.
outliers: Calvin alone doubts the identification of the second messenger, on the ground that a fugitive’s name would have been a reproach.
Barnes turns the phrase one of you into an argument against the slaveholding of his own country and century.
Clarke says outright that one of the two epistles must be wrong about who was the prisoner.
Clarke and Calvin independently argue from this list that Peter was not at Rome.
Ellicott infers that the brethren who held aloof in strife and envy were themselves Jewish Christians.
The editorial matter printed with Calvin answers his doubt from a later writer he never read.

12.pericope_label: Epaphras saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers — Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas, greet you

schools.summary: Ask why the commendation stands here, and answer that to praise a man is itself a sign of love, and that to pray for one is also a sign of love and causes love again; note that the commendation opens a door for his teaching, since reverendness in the teacher is the disciples’ advantage, and that the phrase about his being one of them is added so that they might pride themselves upon the man as producing such men. Weigh the verb: it does not say simply praying but striving, trembling and fearing — and call the witness who bears it a trustworthy witness. Note also that he is commended to the neighbouring cities as well, and that although they would assuredly have heard of him they would learn it too when the letter was read, since the letter was ordered to be read among them.

Render the participle as agonizing, denoting the intense desire he had for their salvation and his fervent earnest pleading for their welfare; take the wish to be that they might maintain their Christian principles unadulterated by philosophy and error and completely perform the will of God, and add that this is the expression of a pious wish without any affirmation that any had been absolutely perfect or would be perfect in this world. Note that the best manuscripts read a word meaning fully convinced or persuaded rather than complete, and think that probably, though not perhaps necessarily, the meaning here; and read the two epithets together as referring again to the pretensions of the Gnostic teachers to exclusive perfection in wisdom, the true fellow-worker praying that this perfection may belong to all and have its basis not in the secrets of heavenly knowledge but in the revealed will of God. Describe the neighbouring city at length: situated under a hill to the north with a large plain to the south, the other city opposite across the plain and the river running between them nearer the latter; celebrated for the hot springs in its vicinity and named for the multitude of its temples; now called by the Turks the Cotton-Tower on account of the white cliffs that lie round it, utterly forsaken and desolate, though the ruins are magnificent enough to show it was once among the most splendid cities in the East. Call it the third of the three cities in the valley that had not seen the apostle’s face, and suppose all three evangelised by the same man and all in peril from the same teachers. Find in one man’s responsibility for three churches, as in the charges of Timothy and Titus, the link between the apostolate of this period and the episcopacy of the future. Then identify the physician with the author of the Gospel and the Acts, note that he was not a Jew by birth but probably a proselyte, supposed a native of Cyrene who died in Achaia soon after the apostle’s martyrdom at the age of eighty-four, and observe that there are incidental evidences in both his books that he was acquainted with the science of medicine and recorded events with the eye of one who practised the healing art. Notice the emphasis of the original, the physician, the beloved one, against the bare name of the next man in the list, and pass on in thought to the last notice of the two together, where one had forsaken the apostle and only the other was with him; say that the affection was not one-sided and that it is beautiful to see preacher and physician warm friends in the community, and add that two evangelists were with the apostle at that moment, possibly with copies of their Gospels with them.

Take the prayer as an example of a good pastor, whom distance of place cannot induce to forget the Church so as to prevent him from carrying the care of it with him beyond the sea; notice the strength of entreaty in the word, and admonish the hearers not to look upon the prayers of their pastor as useless but to reckon that they would afford them no small assistance; and infer that the perfection of Christians is that they should not suspend their scheme of life upon anything else. Bear witness for the man on the ground of having been an eye and ear witness of his fervent prayers, his labour of love and his zealous affection. Then refuse the usual identification of the physician: the evangelist was too well known to stand in need of such a designation and would have been signalised by a more magnificent eulogium, being called a fellow-helper or at least a companion and participant in the apostle’s conflicts; conjecture rather that he was absent at that time and that this is another man of the same name, called a physician to distinguish him from the other. Elsewhere give the evangelist his history and the legend attached to it, that he was of Antioch and a physician of bodies who became a physician of souls, and that some say he was a scholar of Galen, or his sister’s son, who having heard of Christ’s miracles set out with his master for Judea to learn the truth of them, Galen dying on the way while he came to Christ. And say of the next man named that he is undoubtedly the one of whom the apostle afterwards complains that he deserted him.

Render the participle as labouring fervently, and prefer the reading of almost all the manuscripts of the most authentic recension, which have a word meaning fully persuaded where the received text has complete: the noun signifies such a complete persuasion of the certainty of a thing as leaves the mind that has it neither room nor inclination to doubt, and the verb means to be so persuaded, or to persuade thus by demonstrative argument and the exhibition of unquestionable facts — which is the persuasion the Spirit of God gives by means of the gospel, and from which arises the solid happiness of the genuine Christian. Prefer likewise the reading of much labour to that of much zeal in the following verse, the two being nearly of the same meaning though the former appears the better and genuine reading. Name the two neighbouring cities of the province and say that the latter was called the holy city from the multitude of its temples, Apollo and Diana and Esculapius and Hygeia being all worshipped there, as appears from the coins of the city still extant. On the physician, report that he is generally supposed to be the evangelist, though some suppose them different, because where the evangelist is plainly meant he never has more than his simple name, while here a further title is added; and explain the Greek word as signifying a healer, not to be restricted to physician in our narrow sense, since he was surgeon and physician and dispenser of medicines alike, all these being frequently combined in the same person. And leave the trade in the past tense, since such he had been at least, if he was not then; while glossing the perfection as being endued with every Christian grace and the filling as being no longer babes but grown up to the measure of the stature of Christ.

debates: Why the apostle commends the man who prays for them.
Whether the text reads complete or fully persuaded.
What the responsibility for three cities shows about church order.
Whether the physician named here is the evangelist.
What the title beloved physician conveys.
outliers: Calvin denies that this Luke is the evangelist, against every other voice in the chapter.
Clarke and Ellicott independently prefer a variant reading against the received text, and Clarke prefers a second one in the next verse.
Chrysostom explains the commendation as a device to secure a hearing for the man commended.
Ellicott reads the two epithets as aimed at Gnostic claims to exclusive perfection in wisdom.
Ellicott finds in one man’s charge over three cities the germ of the later episcopate.
Gill preserves a legend that Luke was a pupil or nephew of Galen who set out with him to test the miracles.

15.pericope_label: Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea — when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans — the salutation by the hand of me Paul

schools.summary: Report the variety of reading at the first salutation: some manuscripts have the church in his house, some in her house, and the best seem to have in their house, the second requiring a feminine form of the name which the original hardly bears, and the third referring to the man and his family; and conclude that it is not possible to tell whether the house was hers or his. Note that it was not until the third century that separate buildings were used for church worship. Observe that the direction to read this letter in the church, matched by a like direction elsewhere, shows the method by which the apostolic epistles were first published, and that the order to interchange letters with a neighbouring church shows how they became more widely diffused and were recognised as authoritative in the Church at large, and so canonised; add that the likelihood or unlikelihood of such public reading bears importantly on the authenticity of books placed among the doubtful by ancient authorities, and that the public reading of other books was the cause of their being wrongly confused with Holy Scripture. Take the letter from Laodicea to be most likely the circular epistle we call to the Ephesians, one copy going to Laodicea and being passed on as this one was to be. Give the city its history, its earlier names and its renaming by a king in honour of his wife, and its flourishing commerce under Rome. On the pastor addressed, note that the word for his office is the word for a diaconate but used in a more general sense, as in the charge to another minister to make full proof of his ministry, and that the whole tone suggests a ministry of some prominence; deny that any remissness is implied, and take the words as encouragement to increased ardour; add that tradition makes him afterwards a bishop, and that the indirect transmission of a charge is curious, since it seems strange to send through one church a message to a chief pastor of another. And keep to the verb, that fulfilling the ministry means going on filling it full, which is a lifetime job. On the closing autograph, note that the invariable salutation in the apostle’s own hand has become the universal Christian blessing, that in different epistles it is joined to different phrases of blessing or charge, and that in one it expands into a long postscript; say that they were to remember he was suffering on their account and entitled to every expression of sympathy; and remark that the chain clanked afresh as he took the pen to sign, since he was not likely to forget it himself.

Take the household church as a rule rather than an incident: in the instance of one household a rule is laid down as to what it becomes all Christian households to be, that they be so many little churches; let every one know that this charge is laid upon him, that he is to train up his house in the fear of the Lord, keep it under a holy discipline, and in fine form in it the likeness of a Church. Generalise the exchange of letters likewise: though this was addressed to one church it was necessary that it should be profitable to others, and the same must be said of all the epistles, which were in the first instance addressed to particular churches but contain doctrine always in force and common to all ages, so that it is of no importance what title they bear, since the subject matter belongs to us. Deny that the other letter mentioned was written by the apostle, and call it a double mistake to think it was written by him to Laodicea: it was an epistle that had been sent to him, the perusal of which might profit a neighbouring town; and denounce as an exceedingly gross imposture the forgery which some worthless person had the audacity to put forward under that name, so insipid a thing that nothing could be less worthy. On the pastor addressed, conjecture that he was discharging the office during another’s absence and was perhaps not of such a disposition as to be sufficiently diligent without being stirred up; and explain why the charge is sent through the church rather than to him alone, namely that they may know they must themselves employ remonstrances if they see their pastor cold, and that the pastor himself must not refuse to be admonished by the Church — for the ministers of the word are endowed with signal authority, but such as is not exempt from laws, and they must show themselves teachable if they would duly teach others. And say of the closing autograph that it was added after the amanuensis had finished, to prevent all counterfeits and impositions and to assure the churches of the genuineness of the letters.

Explain the household church: this man and his whole family, probably very numerous, appear to have received the gospel, and for their benefit and their neighbours’ he had opened his house for the worship of God — for in those primitive times there were no consecrated places, the simple setting apart of any place for the worship of God being held a sufficient consecration. Take the direction about the neighbouring church to mean that a copy was to be made and sent, which appears to have been a regular custom in the apostolic Church. Then set out the conjectures about the other letter: that it was an epistle sent from Laodicea to the apostle and now forwarded, which is both forced and far-fetched; that the epistle to the Ephesians is the letter in question and was originally directed to Laodicea; or that a distinct letter was sent and is now lost — there being one under that direction in the days of Theodoret and Jerome, though the latter mentions it as apocryphal. Elsewhere say shortly that the letter is from Laodicea and not to it, and that perhaps some letter had been written to the apostle from thence. On the pastor addressed, report that some think him overseer of the church in another’s absence and that he had been remiss, so that the direction appears in the light of reprehension; but answer by a date, that if he is the same man called fellow-labourer and fellow-soldier in the letter written the same year, he cannot have been both at Rome and a delinquent at Colosse at once, so that the words convey no censure but are meant to stir him to further diligence against false teachers. Add that it is the duty of the flock to try them that say they are apostles, to reject the false and to warn as well as receive the true; and define the office against its abuse, since the ministry is not a lordship but a service, a laborious and painful work, an obligation to do and suffer all things and to be the least and the servant of all. And on the closing salutation, say that the preceding part was written by a scribe from the apostle’s mouth while this was written by his own hand, which was how he authenticated every epistle; and that his being in bonds for the gospel was itself the fullest proof of the gospel’s truth, since a cunningly devised fable could not have imposed on such a man.

debates: Whether the house church was held in a man’s house or a woman’s.
What the epistle from Laodicea was.
What the order to exchange letters shows about how the epistles were published.
Whether the message to Archippus is a rebuke.
Why the closing salutation was written in the apostle’s own hand.
outliers: Robertson concludes outright that the gender of the householder cannot be determined.
Calvin and Wesley read the letter as one sent to the apostle from Laodicea; Robertson identifies it with the circular we call Ephesians.
Ellicott draws the formation of the canon out of the direction to exchange letters.
Gill and Calvin take the word to Archippus as reproof; Barnes and Clarke deny that any is implied, Clarke arguing from the date of a companion epistle.
Calvin makes the indirect address a warrant for a congregation to admonish a cold pastor.
Calvin denounces the surviving letter to the Laodiceans as a forgery and an insipid one.
